title: Does synbiotic supplementation improve the effects of a ketogenic diet?
official: The effect of synbiotic supplementation on hypercholesterolaemia during a ketogenic diet: a randomised controlled trial
summary:
Background and study aims
A ketogenic diet involves limiting your carbohydrate intake in food and drinks to less than 50g a day. This is called “ketogenic” because is causes your body to increase the production of ketones (by your liver). Ketones provide energy and also act as important signalling molecules and messengers. Ketogenic diets are being used by millions of people around the world for a variety of different reasons. Some people are using them to help with blood sugar control and/or because they find them helpful for weight management. Others follow a ketogenic diet because of their cognitive and/or neurological effects. In the UK, around 13% of the population are estimated to be following a low carbohydrate diet.
 
Although ketogenic diets are helpful for some outcomes, one potentially negative consequence from consuming a ketogenic diet is an increase in circulating low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol concentrations (“bad cholesterol”). Over years and decades, an increase in LDL cholesterol may increase the risk of cardiovascular disease.
 
Our data indicate that the increase in LDL cholesterol might be due to changes in the composition and function of intestinal microorganisms (e.g., gut bacteria). In the SynKeto project, we will examine if taking a daily supplement (a synbiotic) helps to maintain normal healthy gut bacteria and microorganisms – and whether this prevents the typical increase in LDL cholesterol when people start to follow a ketogenic diet. A synbiotic is a combination of a probiotic and prebiotic fibre (see Appendix). If taking a synbiotic is effective, then it may allow people to get the potential benefits of a ketogenic diet without the potential downsides.

Who can participate?
We are looking for approximately 64 men and women who are aged 18-65 years old, free from any chronic health conditions and dietary restrictions.

What does the study involve?
This study is an intervention study, and the total period of involvement will be over approximately 14 weeks. This includes a 12-week period where participants will have to change their diet and take a daily supplement. During an initial screening visit, we will first check participants are eligible to take part in the study. If participants are eligible and would like to take part, we will ask them to provide written informed consent before we set them up with some equipment to assess diet and physical activity levels, as well as continuous monitors to measure normal glucose and ketone levels. Approximately 1 to 2 weeks later, participants will complete their first main trial visit which will include various measurements including blood, fat and stool samples and body composition scans. After this visit participants will start the 12-week intervention period and will be asked to adhere to a ketogenic diet and daily supplement. Neither the participants nor the research team will be aware who will consume the placebo and who will consume the synbiotic over the 12-week period. After 6 weeks participants will complete an interim visit, involving blood and stool samples and further body composition scans and monitoring of physical activity and glucose and ketone levels. At the end of the 12-week intervention participants will complete a final main trial visit, identical to that completed before the start of the 12-week intervention period.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
By participating in this study individuals will contribute to science and our understanding of how ketogenic diets affect cholesterol, and whether a synbiotic is useful in preventing an increase in LDL cholesterol. This could help millions of people who choose to use ketogenic diets and help clinicians who recommend a ketogenic diet for their patients. 

Participants will also be reimbursed for travel expenses, parking permits and will be provided with a monetary allowance towards groceries for the 12-week intervention period. Participants will also be offered an inconvenience payment in the form of Love2Shop gift vouchers, worth £200, on study completion. 

Finally, participants will be given a copy of some results within 2-4 weeks of completing the study:
•	Diet
•	Physical activity levels
•	Blood pressure
•	Body composition analysis (the amount of muscle and fat that you have, and bone density)
•	Cognitive performance

Where is the study run from?
The study will be run from the Human Physiology Laboratories within the Centre for Nutrition, Exercise & Metabolism at the University of Bath (UK).

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
February 2026 to December 2028.

Who is funding the study?
The study is mainly funded by a government research council, the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC), with a small contribution from a commercial partner (IFF), as part of a BBSRC Industrial Partnership Award.

Who is the main contact?
The Principal Investigator and Primary Contact for this study is Dr Lucy Rogers (LR2013@bath.ac.uk)

DESIGN: The study will be a two-arm, 12‑week, parallel‑group, double‑blind randomised controlled trial (RCT) in men and women aged 18–65 years (N=64)

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Age 18-65 years
2. Body Mass Index (BMI) of 20.0-34.9 kg/m²
3. Able to provide informed consent
4. Willing and able to comply with all study procedures including, maintenance of habitual dietary intake, physical activity, and medication use during the study period.
Exclusion criteria:
1.  Any reported condition or behaviour deemed to either pose undue personal risk to the participant or that would introduce bias and affect study outcomes
2.  Any diagnosed disease(s) or prior surgical procedure that would affect study outcomes (e.g., Type 1 or Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, cholecystectomy)
3.  Severe hypertension (systolic blood pressure ≥ 180 mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure ≥ 120 mmHg)
4.  Taking prescribed medications that will interfere with the study outcomes (e.g., lipid‑lowering medication)
5.  Current use of non‑prescribed supplements that could interfere with the study outcomes (e.g., laxatives)
6.  Use of antibiotic medication in the last 3 months
7.  Frequent use of prebiotic/fibre supplements or probiotic supplements in the last month (>15 times over the past month)
8.  Already consuming a low carbohydrate ketogenic diet
9.  Current or recent tobacco or recreational drug use (within prior 3 months)
10. Known negative reaction to lidocaine anaesthetic and/or taking warfarin
11. Not weight stable in the prior 3 months (>3% weight change)
12. Unable to understand the required instructions
13. Vegetarian or vegan
14. Women: Pregnant or planning to become pregnant
15. Women: Post‑menopausal (absence of menses for >12 months)
